name: Aoki Lock
summary: The Aoki Lock is a rotational foot lock that captures a turned-out foot against the upper body while controlling the leg and hip, potentially stressing both the ankle and knee.
description: Entering the Aoki Lock from Aoki Lock Control keeps the outward-turned foot enclosed and the hip contained. Rehearse the transition without finishing rotation.
overview:
The attacker is seated or on a hip facing the opponent's leg, with the opposing foot turned outward beside the armpit and the hip connection controlled. The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.

Identify the turned-out foot without forcing it to rotate against resistance. Bring the instep under the upper arm and support the heel/Achilles region with the forearm. Secure the upper-body enclosure while leaving the foot unloaded during practice.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Stephan Kesting and Rob Biernacki — the Aoki lock](https://www.grapplearts.com/the-step-by-step-aoki-lock/); [IBJJF — current rule resources](https://ibjjf.com/books-videos).

attacker.name: Aoki Lock Attacker
attacker.description: Aoki Lock (attacker): Identify the turned-out foot without forcing it to rotate against resistance. Bring the instep under the upper arm and support the heel/Achilles region with the forearm.
attacker.overview:
The attacker is seated or on a hip facing the opponent's leg, with the opposing foot turned outward beside the armpit and the hip connection controlled. The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.

Identify the turned-out foot without forcing it to rotate against resistance. Bring the instep under the upper arm and support the heel/Achilles region with the forearm. Secure the upper-body enclosure while leaving the foot unloaded during practice.

Use the legs and hip connection to limit free movement without twisting a planted knee. Recognize that a small body extension can create rotational ankle and knee pressure; do not search for a large finishing movement. Open the arms and leg connection on a tap, sudden turn, or loss of communication.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Hip control contains the leg while the outward-turned foot is enclosed beside the upper arm. Keep that connection stable during control-only rehearsal and open it fully before the partner turns or stands.

A change from this rotated-foot capture to another leg lock is a new submission entry. Unload and open the Aoki grip first, then inspect the replacement foot orientation and hip connection before any pressure is added.

Once the rotated foot and hip are connected, even a small bridging motion can load the lock. Keep the hips quiet in control-only rehearsal and open the enclosure before the partner changes position; this bridge applies finishing force rather than creating escape space.

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): Which foot orientation supplies this capture?
flashcards.answer: Identify the turned-out foot without forcing it to rotate against resistance.
flashcards.answer_line: Turned outward beside the upper body

plausible: Straight along the forearm, unturned
Turned inward beneath the upper arm

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): Where do the upper arm and forearm contact the foot?
flashcards.answer: Bring the instep under the upper arm and support the heel/Achilles region with the forearm.
flashcards.answer_line: Arm over instep, forearm under heel

plausible: Heel under armpit, instep on forearm
Arm over ankle, forearm high on calf
trap: Both hands on forefoot, heel outside

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): What is the purpose of connecting the arms around the foot?
flashcards.answer: Secure the upper-body enclosure while leaving the foot unloaded during practice.
flashcards.answer_line: Hold instep and heel at your torso

plausible: Pin heel with instep outside the arm
Hold instep, leave a gap under heel
trap: Let the foot turn freely in the grip

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): What do your legs control in addition to the foot grip?
flashcards.answer: Use the legs and hip connection to limit free movement without twisting a planted knee.
flashcards.answer_line: The opponent's hip and leg movement

plausible: Only ankle movement in the arm grip
Only knee bend, leaving the hip free
trap: Only free leg, captured hip free

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): Why can a small bridge already load this lock?
flashcards.answer: Recognize that a small body extension can create rotational ankle and knee pressure; do not search for a large finishing movement.
flashcards.answer_line: Foot turns against a restrained hip

plausible: Only the calf muscle is compressed
Foot bends straight, hip stays free
trap: Heel slips free as the torso extends

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): The partner taps while their leg is entangled. What opens?
flashcards.answer: Open the arms and leg connection on a tap, sudden turn, or loss of communication.
flashcards.answer_line: Both arm enclosure and leg restraint

plausible: Just top hand, armpit still tight
Just hip frame, heel still enclosed
trap: Both hands, arm still pins instep

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): Where is the attacker relative to the captured leg?

plausible: On a hip, held foot behind the torso
Seated facing away from their legs
trap: Seated past the foot, hip unattached

flashcards.question: Aoki Lock (attacker): What distinguishes Aoki from a calf slicer?
flashcards.answer: The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.
flashcards.answer_line: Foot rotation, not a knee fulcrum

plausible: Bent-knee pressure, not foot capture
Linear ankle extension, no rotation

defender.name: Aoki Lock Defender
defender.description: Aoki Lock (defender): Treat an outward-turned foot caught by the upper body as a rotational lock rather than an ordinary straight ankle lock. Hand fight and recover foot position before the attacker connects around the foot.
defender.overview:
The attacker is seated or on a hip facing the opponent's leg, with the opposing foot turned outward beside the armpit and the hip connection controlled. The foot enclosure creates rotation rather than a bent-knee calf compression. A foot offered on the hip during an ashi exchange can supply the capture, but the position name alone does not establish it.

Treat an outward-turned foot caught by the upper body as a rotational lock rather than an ordinary straight ankle lock. Hand fight and recover foot position before the attacker connects around the foot. Do not rotate the torso independently of a captured foot and knee.

Create slack in the hand and hip controls before withdrawing the leg. Stop at a secure rotational capture rather than testing whether the joint still tolerates movement. Wait for the entire enclosure to open before standing, turning, or restarting the exchange.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

The early escape removes the hand enclosure and the leg entanglement while the foot and knee can still stay aligned. Once released, bring the freed knee back toward the torso and recover a facing frame before restarting the exchange.
